What Dr. Moore says to focus on For each modality: indications, general types, and interpretation. He says you do not need to know ultrasound technique or the names of the radionuclides, the detailed imaging signs separating an abscess from other lesions, or phases beyond the basics. Points I added that aren't in his slides or narration are tagged beyond source; spots where I fixed or clarified something are tagged corrected.

1. Big Picture: Which Test When

His one-slide study guide

Clinical questionImaging of choice
Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis)Non-contrast CT (NCCT) of abdomen/pelvis. KUB if CT not available. (Renal US is quick but visualization is limited.)
Renal mass (suspicious for RCC)Contrast-enhanced CT of abdomen/pelvis, or MRI with and without contrast (slower, less available)
Hydronephrosis (obstruction)Ultrasound or CT urography
Renal artery stenosisCT angiography or MR angiography
HematuriaCystoscopy preferred; imaging of choice is CT urography for gross hematuria
Function/perfusion of each kidney separately (scarring, transplant)Scintigraphy
Recurrent UTI, especially in childrenVCUG (posterior urethral valves, vesicoureteral reflux)

Anatomy you must be able to place

  • Kidneys sit in the retroperitoneum (posterior/deep). The right kidney is slightly lower than the left (liver).
  • Renal arteries come off the aorta near the mesenteric arteries; ureters run from the renal pelvis down to the bladder; renal pelvis → major calyces → minor calyces; parenchyma = cortex + medulla; surrounded by a capsule.
  • Plain films don't outline the ureters: know their path so you don't dismiss a stone along it.
  • Three places stones get stuck (narrowest points): (1) ureteropelvic junction (renal pelvis), (2) where the ureter crosses the great (iliac) vessels, and (3) the ureterovesical junction (entering the bladder).
Stone-impaction sites: renal pelvis (A), crossing the great vessels (B), entry into the bladder (C)

Modality comparison

ModalityShowsRadiationContrastKey use
KUBStructure (calcified stones, gas, foreign bodies)LowNoneQuick screen
NCCTStructureSignificant (slide: 20–40 mSv)NoneStones
CT with IV contrast / CTUStructure + some functionHigher (more phases)IV iodinatedMass, infection, collecting system
CTA / MRAVesselsCT: yes. MRI: noneIVRAS, aneurysm, RVT, trauma
UltrasoundStructure, flow (Doppler)NoneNoneHydronephrosis, cysts, CKD, pregnancy
ScintigraphyFunction, perfusion, drainageRelatively lowRadiotracerSplit function, scarring, obstruction
VCUGDynamic bladder/urethraLow with pulsed fluoroscopy (radionuclide version lowest)Intravesical, via catheterReflux, valves
Structure vs functionA plain film or non-contrast CT shows structure (function can only be inferred). Adding IV contrast starts to show function (blood in, processing, excretion). For true kidney-by-kidney function, go to scintigraphy.

2. KUB & IVP

KUB (Kidneys, Ureters, Bladder)

  • Plain abdominal X-ray with a plane of focus targeting kidneys, ureters, bladder (spine, bowel still visible). A quick initial look at the urinary and GI systems.
  • Indications: abdominal pain, suspected kidney stones, bowel obstruction or perforation, other urinary issues (bladder stones, anatomical abnormalities).
  • Advantages: fast, accessible, relatively low radiation. Limits: poor soft-tissue detail, small lesions missed, structures overlap (hard to know depth).
  • Views: single supine view (standard). Gravity on a supine film: fluid settles toward the back; air rises toward the front of the patient (the "surface" of the image, not the top of the film). For air-fluid levels add an upright view (air moves to the top of the image) or a decubitus view (patient on side).

Interpretation

  • Radiopaque (bright) shadows = renal/ureteral calculi (calcium-containing), bladder stones (pelvis).
  • Bowel gas pattern: air-fluid levels = possible obstruction. (Slide: absent bowel gas may suggest perforation.) beyond source The classic perforation sign is free air under the diaphragm, best on an upright film.
  • Foreign bodies: stents, catheters, surgical clips.
  • Normal landmarks: liver RUQ (extends left past midline), spleen LUQ (similar density to liver), psoas muscles, kidneys. Right kidney sits lower.
  • Stones that are not high in calcium aren't well seen on KUB (corrected these are radiolucent, not "radiopaque"). Historically you'd outline them with an IVP.
KUB: liver (purple), spleen (green), psoas, kidneys (orange/red), bladder (blue)
KUB with a ureteral stone (arrow). Overlying bowel gas makes it easy to miss
Staghorn calculus: a large stone filling the upper collecting system (a "branched" stone; not all are calcium-dense)

IVP (intravenous pyelogram)

  • IV contrast filters into the collecting system and outlines it. A blockage or stone appears as a dark filling defect with contrast going around it, or contrast stops at the obstruction.
  • Largely replaced by CT: an IVP took an hour or more (serial KUB films, contrast must perfuse, be excreted, outline the system); a CT stone protocol takes ~1–2 minutes.
  • Ureters look different caliber from moment to moment because of peristalsis; that is not hydroureter. Hydroureter/hydronephrosis = marked dilation behind an obstruction.
IVP: kidneys, ureters, bladder outlined; kidney stone in Figure 2
IVP: contrast in the upper collecting system but not beyond, due to an obstructing stone

3. Renal CT: Non-contrast, Contrast & CT Urogram

Indications

Kidney stones • suspected masses/tumors • trauma • hematuria evaluation • preoperative planning for kidney surgery.

Non-contrast CT (NCCT): the stone test

  • Best for detecting kidney stones and the most commonly used test in the ED for suspected stones. Fast, no iodinated contrast (no allergy or contrast-nephropathy risk). Slide: 20–40 mSv radiation exposure.
  • Appearance: calcium-containing structures are bright white (bone, calcified stones); air is black; soft tissues in grays. A stone is a bright white spot in the ureter or kidney.
  • Look for secondary signs: dilated ureter and collecting system (hydronephrosis) above the stone. Tumors (including adjacent structures) can also obstruct.
NCCT: ureteral calculus (arrow)
Ureteral stone with hydronephrosis (dilated collecting system above it)
Stone at the ureterovesical junction and a dilated ureter above it

CT with IV contrast

  • Best for vascular structures, tumors, infections, cysts, hydronephrosis, trauma, and abnormal enhancement. Phases: arterial (contrast in renal arteries, early perfusion) → venous (renal veins) → delayed / excretory (collecting system filled). Dual- or triple-phase CT is used in cancer work-up.
  • Use IV contrast, not oral. Oral contrast is for the GI tract and can obscure the kidneys/collecting system.
  • Safety: radiation, and check renal function (GFR, creatinine) before contrast; iodinated contrast can harm the kidneys and some people are allergic. More phases = more radiation.
  • Contrast CT gives an idea of function (blood in, processed, excreted); for more precise function use scintigraphy.
  • Low-calcium stones that aren't seen on a plain film may need contrast. beyond source In practice, modern NCCT detects nearly all stones; contrast/urography is used to outline the collecting system.

Pathology on contrast CT

FindingWhat you seeThink
Wedge-shaped hypo-enhancement + fever, abdominal/flank painA wedge of the kidney enhances less than the restPyelonephritis (infection)
Mass separate from the parenchyma, enhances less than normal kidney, distinct capsule/bordersNon-enhancing/low-enhancing lesionRenal cell carcinoma
Pocket of low enhancement with a rimRing-enhancing fluid collectionRenal abscess (no need to know the finer imaging signs)
Dilated collecting systemHydronephrosisObstruction (stone, tumor)
Wedge-shaped hypoenhancement: pyelonephritis
Renal cell carcinoma: enhances less than the kidney (arrow)
Renal abscess: low-enhancing pocket with a rim

CT urogram (CTU)

  • Contrast CT with an excretory (delayed) phase: focuses on contrast excreted into the renal pelvis and out through the collecting system. Reconstructions give a clear view of the collecting system.
  • Uses: hydronephrosis from obstruction, filling defects, urothelial lesions; imaging of choice for gross hematuria (cystoscopy preferred for the bladder).
CT urogram reconstruction: collecting system and ureters to the bladder
CTU: left distal ureteral stone (arrow) with hydronephrosis

4. Renal CT Angiogram (CTA)

Indications

Suspected renal artery stenosis • renal vein thrombosis • vascular malformations/aneurysms • planning renal surgery or transplant • evaluation of difficult-to-control (secondary) hypertension • trauma. High-resolution, non-invasive, quick.

Phases (timing from contrast injection)

PhaseTimingUse
Non-contrastBaselineComparison
Arterial~15–25 sRenal arteries, stenosis
Venous~30–60 sRenal veins, surrounding venous structures
Delayed (excretory)LaterParenchyma, collecting system, some masses and urothelial tumors

Findings

FindingAppearance
Renal artery stenosisFocal narrowing, with post-stenotic dilation
Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)"String of beads" irregular renal artery; look for it in difficult-to-control hypertension (classically younger women beyond source)
Renal aneurysmOutpouching of the artery or branches
Renal vein thrombosisFilling defect in the renal vein
Tumor invasionTumor encroaching/compressing renal vessels
Renal infarctionWedge of non-enhancement (no perfusion) from arterial occlusion or emboli; a complication of FMD/stenosis
Traumatic renal artery transectionTruncated artery, no enhancement of the kidney, and contrast/blood extravasating into the retroperitoneum (fluid collection)
VariantsAccessory renal arteries, aberrant vessels (planning transplant/surgery)
Normal CTA: aorta and renal artery with branches
Fibromuscular dysplasia: irregular "string of beads" renal artery (left) vs smooth artery (right)
Renal infarction: wedge of non-enhancement
Artery stenosis with a large infarct (little enhancement)
Traumatic renal artery transection: no kidney enhancement
Same injury: blood in the retroperitoneum (arrow)

5. Renal Ultrasound

Indications & features

  • Indications: kidney stones, hydronephrosis, cysts/tumors/abscesses, renal failure / CKD, Doppler for renal artery/vein flow, and guidance for biopsy or drainage.
  • Advantages: no ionizing radiation, real-time, inexpensive, widely available, safe for everyone including pregnancy. Limits: body habitus and bowel gas; less detail than CT/MRI.
  • Coverage: it images the kidneys well, and the bladder and lower (distal) ureter well. The mid-ureter is very hard to see (overlying bowel). So: abnormality in the kidney or just above/in the bladder, good chance; in between, you won't see it.
  • Types: conventional (primary), Doppler (flow, RAS, thrombosis, perfusion; also ureteric jets), 3D if available. You don't need to know the technique.
  • Position note: the left kidney sits a bit higher/more posterior than the right (spleen is smaller than the liver).

Normal vs abnormal

FindingUltrasound appearance
Normal kidneySmooth bean shape, 9–12 cm, visible corticomedullary differentiation (cortex, medullary pyramids, central pelvis/fat appears white)
HydronephrosisDilated, hypoechoic (black) urine starting at the central pelvis and growing outward like a plant; severity: mild (pelvis dilated, pyramids still separate) → moderate (pelvis connects to pyramids) → severe (architecture smudged; pelvis and medulla indistinguishable). Rarely free fluid around the capsule if a calyx ruptures.
Kidney stoneHyperechoic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing; asymptomatic until it moves/obstructs. Twinkling artifact on color Doppler supports a stone. Staghorn = large branching stone with shadowing.
Obstructing stone at the UVJBladder color Doppler: ureteral jet present on the normal side, absent on the obstructed side (watch ~5 minutes to be sure)
Simple cystAnechoic, round, well-defined, posterior enhancement; peripheral (doesn't originate from the central pelvis)
Tumor / RCCSolid, irregular, heterogeneous echotexture; non-cystic
Renal failure / CKDSmall, echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation
DopplerNormal arterial/venous flow; stenosis, thrombosis, or reduced perfusion show abnormal flow
Don't mix these upHydronephrosis = dark fluid starting from the central pelvis and expanding outward. Cyst = round fluid collection on the periphery. RCC = solid lump. (Figures below come from the ScholarRx Brick, not Dr. Moore's slides, since his ultrasound examples are videos.)
Hydronephrosis (dilated calyces/pelvis)
Multiple cysts (polycystic kidney disease)
Chronic kidney disease (left, small echogenic) vs normal (right)

6. Renal Scintigraphy (Nuclear Renal Scan)

  • Purpose: function, perfusion and drainage. Images are fuzzy (no fine anatomic detail), but you can quantify perfusion and function for each kidney individually, which blood tests, contrast CT or MRI can't do accurately.
  • Indications: suspected renal artery stenosis; renal scarring (e.g. chronic infection); obstruction and drainage (hydronephrosis); split renal function (before nephrectomy); transplant evaluation (rejection/obstruction); determining level of renal failure. Relatively low radiation.
TypeAgent (names not required)Shows
StaticTc-99m DMSACortical anatomy → scarring = areas of reduced uptake. Normal = homogeneous uptake in both kidneys
DynamicTc-99m MAG3 or DTPAPerfusion phase (blood flow right after injection), functional phase (uptake and excretion), time-activity curves. Obstruction = delayed excretion with tracer accumulating in pelvis/calyces
Function scansDTPA / MAG3Calculate GFR or effective renal plasma flow (ERPF)
TransplantMAG3Rejection or obstruction
Normal dynamic renal scan (perfusion then excretion)
Perfusion and function curves with split function per kidney

7. Voiding Cystourethrogram (VCUG)

  • Fluoroscopy (real-time) of the bladder and urethra during filling and voiding. Evaluates the lower urinary tract for structural abnormalities and vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
  • Indications: recurrent UTIs, especially in children; known/suspected VUR; posterior urethral valves and other urethral abnormalities; pre-/post-operative evaluation.
  • Types: standard VCUG (contrast + X-ray; detailed anatomy; pulsed fluoroscopy limits radiation) vs radionuclide VCUG (radiotracer; lowest dose, often for children and follow-up; good for detecting reflux but less anatomic detail).
  • Technique: scout film → radiopaque contrast instilled through a catheter (early filling, full bladder: capacity, wall integrity, reflux) → catheter removed → voiding phase (urethra, retrograde flow) → post-void films for residual dye. Use proper sterile catheter technique.
FindingAppearance
NormalSmooth bladder wall, uniform filling, no contrast backing into the ureters; smooth, open urethra without narrowing
Vesicoureteral refluxContrast flows backward from the bladder into ureters and possibly the kidneys; graded I (mild) to V (severe). Severe cases: dilated ureters and collecting systems (hydronephrosis)
Posterior urethral valvesNarrowing/obstruction of the posterior urethra, with dilation of the urethra proximal (upstream) to it. beyond source Occurs in boys; can cause hydronephrosis and recurrent UTI
Bladder diverticulaOutpouchings of the bladder wall (filling defects during filling)
Urethral strictureSegment of narrowing that restricts flow during voiding
Normal voiding phase: smooth bladder and urethral outline
Posterior urethral valve: narrowing with a dilated urethra proximal to it
Vesicoureteral reflux: unilateral retrograde flow into the collecting system
Severe bilateral reflux: dilated ureters and collecting systems

8. Clinical Scenarios

If the question is...Reach for...Why
Suspected stone in the EDNCCT (KUB if unavailable)Fast, most sensitive for calcified stones
Stone/hydronephrosis, pregnant or radiation-sensitive; quick bedside lookUltrasoundNo radiation; good for hydronephrosis, stones in kidney/near bladder; poor mid-ureter
Renal massContrast CT (or MRI)Enhancement pattern separates solid mass from cyst
Fever + flank pain, kidney imagingContrast CTWedge hypoenhancement (pyelo); abscess
Gross hematuriaCT urography (+ cystoscopy)Collecting system + parenchyma
Resistant hypertension, ?RAS or FMDCTA or MRAVessel narrowing, string of beads
Sudden severe flank pain with a non-enhancing wedgeContrast CT/CTARenal infarction (embolus, stenosis)
Trauma, no kidney enhancementContrast CT/CTAArtery transection, retroperitoneal bleed
Need function of each kidney (nephrectomy, transplant, scarring)ScintigraphyQuantifies split function and drainage
Child with recurrent UTIsVCUGPosterior urethral valves, vesicoureteral reflux
Rising creatinine, rule out obstructionRenal ultrasoundHydronephrosis; also small echogenic kidneys = CKD
Contrast reminderAdd contrast → more images (more radiation) plus iodinated contrast risk (allergy, kidney injury). Always check GFR/creatinine first, which ties directly to your lab guide.

9. Final High-Yield Table

ModalityRemember
KUBQuick, low radiation, supine; calcified stones radiopaque; ureters invisible (know their path); low-calcium stones missed; upright/decubitus for air-fluid. Stone sites: UPJ, iliac crossing, UVJ.
IVPContrast outlines collecting system; filling defect/cut-off; long and largely replaced by CT.
NCCTStone test of choice; calcium bright; look for hydronephrosis; no contrast; significant radiation.
Contrast CTMasses (RCC enhances less), pyelonephritis (wedge), abscess (rim); phases arterial → venous → delayed; IV not oral; check GFR.
CT urogramExcretory phase; hydronephrosis, filling defects; gross hematuria.
CTARAS (post-stenotic dilation), FMD (string of beads), aneurysm, RVT (filling defect), infarct (wedge), transection (no enhancement + retroperitoneal blood).
UltrasoundNo radiation; kidney and bladder yes, mid-ureter no. Hydronephrosis, stone (shadowing, twinkling), cyst (anechoic), RCC (solid), CKD (small echogenic).
ScintigraphyFunction. DMSA = scars; MAG3 = perfusion/excretion/obstruction/transplant; split function before nephrectomy.
VCUGRecurrent UTI in kids: reflux (grade I–V) and posterior urethral valves; also diverticula, strictures. Radionuclide version = lowest dose.

Sources: Dr. John E. Moore, DO, Renal II Imaging Parts 1 & 2 (slides and video narration); ScholarRx Brick Renal Laboratory Tests and Imaging (ultrasound figures). Items tagged "beyond source" are standard teaching points I added.
